passage:
Note to file, Friday.

Nazia, our junior executive, received a letter of queries from the tax office on Monday, and I watched how it was handled. Nazia read the letter twice, listed the three documents asked for, and checked each figure against our ledger before drafting anything. The reply was polite: "With reference to your letter, please find the details attached." There was no muttering about the clerk or the process; the letter was treated as a set of rules to meet.

One invoice turned out to have been filed late. Nazia said so plainly in the reply instead of leaving it out. It went out two days before the last date. I asked what would have happened if the invoice had been hidden. "It would have cost us more later," Nazia said. I am keeping this reply as our template.

Bidisha, office manager

qa.q: How many documents did Nazia list from the letter?
qa.a: Nazia listed the three documents asked for.

qa.q: How did Nazia seem to feel about the tax office's queries, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nazia seemed calm and unbothered, reading the letter twice, checking each figure and replying politely without muttering about the clerk or the process.

qa.q: What could a new colleague learn from this reply about answering an official letter?
qa.a: Read the letter carefully, check the figures, be polite and accurate in writing, and send the reply before the last date.

qa.q: How might a clerk at the tax office see a reply like this?
qa.a: A clerk would likely find it easy to process because it is clear, polite and complete, and may treat the firm as cooperative.

grounding: Nazia treats the tax process as a system with rules, replies on time, accurately and politely, and is honest about the late invoice.
